title: Litvinenko and FSB Officers Denounce the Agency at 1998 Press Conference
description_short: Litvinenko and other FSB officers publicly denounced the agency in Moscow in 1998.
description_medium: A U.K. public inquiry records that Alexander Litvinenko and other officers publicly denounced the Federal Security Service at a Moscow press conference on November 17, 1998. The inquiry says the officers had concerns about orders involving Boris Berezovsky. The supplied sources establish the historical event but do not establish a connection to Donald Trump, so this is an internal, publication-ineligible draft.
description_long: The U.K. public inquiry into Alexander Litvinenko’s death says Litvinenko and colleagues were unhappy with orders they had received, particularly orders involving Boris Berezovsky. It identifies a Moscow press conference on November 17, 1998, as the culmination of their response, where Litvinenko and other officers publicly denounced the Federal Security Service before international media. The inquiry records the meeting and the participants’ concerns; it does not establish that the alleged orders were carried out. The supplied TrumpFile page describes accusations voiced at the conference, but those allegations remain attributed and are not findings. The event itself is unrelated to Donald Trump in the materials reviewed, and no direct or indirect Trump connection has been established for this chronology. The previous Washington Post link predates the event and concerns a separate subject, so it does not provide the missing connection. This neutral rewrite preserves the documented press conference while removing Trump framing and the unsupported impact claims. It remains an internal draft until its relevance to this project can be established.

title: State Department Official Requested Records About Journalists and Trump Critics
description_short: A State Department official sought internal records involving journalists and Trump critics.
description_medium: MIT Technology Review reported that a March 11, 2025 document from Trump appointee Darren Beattie requested State Department staff emails and other records involving journalists, researchers, organizations focused on foreign disinformation, and Trump critics. The request concerned records from the R/FIMI Hub. The reporting does not establish that intelligence agencies compiled the surveillance, financial, communications, or family dossiers alleged in the original entry.
description_long: MIT Technology Review reported that a document dated March 11, 2025, and distributed in person to State Department employees in early March sought emails and other records from staff of the Counter Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference Hub (R/FIMI). The requested material concerned people and organizations that tracked or wrote about foreign disinformation, as well as critics of President Donald Trump and his allies; the report named journalists and former officials among those referenced. Trump appointee Darren Beattie framed the request as a transparency initiative, according to the article. This is a documented internal records request by a State Department official. It does not establish that a White House-wide directive reached intelligence or law-enforcement agencies, or that dossiers containing surveillance records, financial information, private communications, and family material were actually compiled. The report also does not document a resulting investigation or publication of those records. This entry is narrowed to the reported request and keeps its scope and effects distinct from the unsupported claims in the frozen version.

original_title: Trump bans encrypted messaging apps for federal employees over spying concerns

source_fact_map.fact: Reuters reported on the Trump administration’s use of Signal, contradicting the frozen record’s categorical assertion that the administration banned employees from using encrypted messaging apps.
source_fact_map.quote: The Trump administration sought to put the scandal over its use of the Signal messaging app behind it on Monday
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: WASHINGTON, March 31 (Reuters) - The Trump administration sought to put the scandal over its use of the Signal messaging app behind it on Monday, calling it case closed, even as the breach provoked bipartisan criticism and opened up divisions inside the White House.

source_fact_map.fact: NARA says federal employees may conduct official business on third-party messaging apps subject to federal recordkeeping rules.
source_fact_map.quote: Officers or employees of federal agencies may conduct official business using third-party messaging apps.
source_fact_map.source_excerpt: Officers or employees of federal agencies may conduct official business using third-party messaging apps. However, the FRA imposes strict requirements on the use of personal accounts to conduct agency business. If any agency employee uses a personal account to engage in official business, they must: (1) copy their official account when creating or sending the message, or (2) forward a complete copy of the record to an official account within 20 days. 44 U.S.C. § 2911.

Successful; Reuters article states that the controversy concerned the administration’s use of Signal. The earlier Firecrawl scrape attempt timed out with HTTP 504.
Successful; NARA memorandum says officers or employees may conduct official business using third-party messaging apps while meeting records requirements.

blockers: No source in the supplied record establishes a government-wide Trump administration ban on Signal, WhatsApp, or other encrypted messaging apps; the frozen record also supplies no source for its claim that the purpose was to monitor internal dissent.

Reuters documents senior administration officials’ Signal use, and NARA guidance explicitly permits official business on third-party messaging apps subject to records rules. The available sources do not support the categorical ban in the title.

The supplied research notes identify a separate June 2025 WhatsApp restriction for U.S. House staff devices. That action was issued by the House chief administrative officer, not the Trump administration, and cannot be substituted for this claim.
uncertainties: Agency-specific restrictions may exist; the retrieved material does not establish a government-wide prohibition or prove that no narrower agency policy existed.
No evidence supports the frozen entry’s stated surveillance motive or cybersecurity consequences.

impact_proposal.confidence_reason: The alleged ban is unsupported and contradicted by reporting of official Signal use and NARA guidance; no coherent impact score can be assigned to the unsupported blanket-ban event.
impact_proposal.rationale: The evidence supports an exclusion candidate for the categorical ban claim, not a verified ban event. Scoring the original claim would imply a policy action and motive that the sources do not establish.
impact_proposal.basis: Reuters reports administration use of Signal; NARA guidance allows official use of third-party apps subject to records requirements.
impact_proposal.notes: No zero score assigned; narrower agency rules and the unsupported motive remain unresolved.
